# Lockfile discipline

`package.json` holds ranges. The lockfile holds the exact tree that was resolved and reviewed. An install that's allowed to rewrite the lockfile in CI or in a Docker build can ship a tree nobody reviewed, including a newly published, compromised patch release that falls inside a `^` range.

`llm-package-hallucination` covers whether a new package should be added at all. This rule covers how the resolved tree is pinned and reproduced once it is.

## Rules

- Commit the lockfile, together with the `package.json` change that produced it. Never add a lockfile to `.gitignore`.
- Keep one package manager and one lockfile per project. A frozen install verifies only its own manager's lockfile (`npm ci` reads `package-lock.json` or `npm-shrinkwrap.json`), so a second lockfile drifts unchecked. `npm install` can even resolve from a stray `yarn.lock`.
- In CI and Dockerfiles, install with the frozen command so a lockfile that's out of sync with `package.json` fails the build instead of being rewritten:
  - npm: `npm ci`, not `npm install`.
  - pnpm: `pnpm install --frozen-lockfile`.
  - Yarn 2+: `yarn install --immutable`. Yarn 1 (classic): `yarn install --frozen-lockfile`.
- Change dependencies through the package manager (`npm install <pkg>@<version>`, `pnpm add`, `yarn add`). The lockfile is generated output, so let the tool write it.
- Review lockfile diffs in PRs. A package or resolved URL that no `package.json` change explains needs an explanation before merge.
- On npm projects, run `npm audit signatures` after `npm ci` in CI. It checks registry signatures and provenance attestations for the installed packages.

## Examples

```yaml
# BAD — CI may resolve a different tree than the one committed
- run: npm install
- run: npm test

# GOOD — install exactly the committed tree, then verify it came from the registry intact
- run: npm ci
- run: npm audit signatures
- run: npm test
```

```dockerfile
# BAD — lockfile not copied, so the image resolves ranges at build time
COPY package.json ./
RUN npm install

# GOOD — frozen install from the committed lockfile
COPY package.json package-lock.json ./
RUN npm ci --omit=dev
```

## Gotchas

- pnpm turns on `--frozen-lockfile` and Yarn turns on `--immutable` automatically in CI environments. Write the flag anyway, so the Dockerfile and local reproduction scripts behave the same as CI.
- `npm ci` deletes an existing `node_modules` before installing, and it can't add individual packages. Use it for installs, never for changing dependencies.
- A failing `npm ci` because `package.json` and the lockfile disagree is the signal working. Fix it by running `npm install` locally and committing the updated lockfile, not by switching CI back to `npm install`.

## Source

- npm — `npm ci`: <https://docs.npmjs.com/cli/v11/commands/npm-ci> (lockfile required, errors on mismatch, never writes `package.json` or the lockfile, removes `node_modules`).
- npm — `package-lock.json`: <https://docs.npmjs.com/cli/v11/configuring-npm/package-lock-json> ("intended to be committed into source repositories"; describes the exact tree so later installs are identical).
- npm — `npm audit` (`audit signatures`): <https://docs.npmjs.com/cli/v11/commands/npm-audit>.
- npm — `npm install` (lockfile precedence, including `yarn.lock`): <https://docs.npmjs.com/cli/v11/commands/npm-install>.
- pnpm — `pnpm install --frozen-lockfile` (default `true` in CI): <https://pnpm.io/cli/install#--frozen-lockfile>.
- Yarn — `yarn install --immutable` (defaults to true on CI): <https://yarnpkg.com/cli/install>; Yarn 1 `--frozen-lockfile`: <https://classic.yarnpkg.com/en/docs/cli/install>.
